subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Mentor's note, hostel year group. On Monday Nandini came to me shaken. A cruel post about a first-year had sat in the 120-member hostel chat for six hours, with forty reactions and no reports. Nandini said, "I saw it in the morning and thought somebody must have flagged it already." The sender, Ojas, had not been named by anyone. Nandini realised each reader had thought the same. We reported it to the warden together that hour, and the warden spoke with the first-year and the sender before evening. I told Nandini that assuming someone else has reported is very common, and that being the one who does is useful, not silly. — Meena Ma'am

qa.q: How many members were in the hostel chat?
qa.a: The hostel chat had 120 members.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when coming to the mentor on Monday?
qa.a: Nandini was shaken and guilty, having assumed someone else would report the post; realising everyone had thought the same made the assumption feel heavy.

qa.q: What turning point did Nandini and the mentor take that hour?
qa.a: They reported the post to the warden together straight away, and the warden spoke with the first-year and the sender before evening.

qa.q: What might the first-year have been going through during the six hours the post stayed in the chat?
qa.a: The first-year may have felt exposed and humiliated with no sign anyone cared, as forty people reacted and nobody reported.

grounding: A student sees a cruel post in a big group chat and assumes someone else will report it, since the bigger the group the smaller each person's felt duty.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Saturday. Somebody put a photo of Vandana with a cruel caption in the big class chat, ninety people. My thumb hovered over the report button. Then I thought: with ninety of us, surely someone has already done it. I put the phone down and made tea. An hour later the photo was still there and Vandana had left the chat. That was when I felt sick. I hit report, then messaged Vandana: "I saw it. I am sorry I waited. Do you want to tell our class teacher together?" She wrote back "ok". We called the teacher that evening. The teacher answered, asked for screenshots, and got the post taken down before night. — Anirban

qa.q: How many people were in the class chat?
qa.a: The class chat had ninety people.

qa.q: Why did Anirban put the phone down without reporting the photo?
qa.a: Anirban assumed that with ninety people someone else must have reported it, so the felt duty was small; the sick feeling came later when Vandana left the chat.

qa.q: What choice did Anirban make once the sick feeling arrived?
qa.a: Anirban reported the photo, apologised to Vandana and offered to call the class teacher together, which turned regret into action.

qa.q: What might Vandana have felt when leaving the chat and later reading Anirban's message?
qa.a: Vandana was probably hurt and humiliated on leaving, and may have felt some comfort at the message, though the plain "ok" shows caution.

grounding: A student sees a cruel post in a big group chat and assumes someone else will report it, then acts once the harm is clear.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
The college group chat in the small town had nearly two hundred members. At eleven at night, Dhruv posted a video: a first-year from the next village, drunk and stumbling on the railway bridge, while the boys filming laughed.
Raghav watched it twice. Twenty people had already seen it. Someone will tell someone, he thought. It's not my job.
Then he looked again. The boy was still on that bridge, maybe, right now.
Raghav called the college warden, who picked up on the second ring. The warden phoned the boy's family and the railway police, and within half an hour the boy was at home. Raghav then reported the video and asked Dhruv to delete it. He sat on his bed, heart racing, thinking how close he'd come to scrolling past.

qa.q: Where was the first-year stumbling?
qa.a: He was stumbling on the railway bridge.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling as he sat on his bed?
qa.a: He felt shaken and anxious, his heart racing at how close he came to scrolling past.

qa.q: What did Raghav do right once he stopped waiting?
qa.a: He called the warden at once, which got the boy's family and the railway police involved, and then reported the video.

qa.q: How might the first-year feel the next day, seeing the video?
qa.a: He would likely feel ashamed and exposed, but safer knowing someone got help instead of just laughing.

grounding: Shows a student who sees a dangerous video in a big group chat, first assumes someone else will act, then calls for help.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
The university housing chat in Prague had over three hundred students. Emil posted a clip of a classmate, Tomas, stammering through a presentation, with a mocking caption. Laughing faces piled up underneath.
Ivan saw it on the tram. He frowned. Somebody from Tomas's course will report it, he thought. There are hundreds of us.
Two stops later, nothing had changed. The clip had more views, not fewer.
Ivan reported the post to the chat moderators and wrote to Emil privately: “Please take that down. It's not fair to him.” Then he messaged Tomas: “Saw the clip. That's not okay. You alright?”
Tomas replied an hour later: “Thanks. Nobody else said anything.” The moderators removed the clip that evening.

qa.q: Where was Ivan when he saw the clip?
qa.a: He saw it on the tram.

qa.q: What was Ivan thinking when he first saw the post?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable but assumed someone from Tomas's course would report it, since there were hundreds of students.

qa.q: What small steps did Ivan take, and why were they useful?
qa.a: He reported the post, asked Emil privately to take it down and checked on Tomas, which were quick, safe ways to help.

qa.q: How might Tomas have felt when nobody else said anything?
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and alone, and grateful that at least one person reached out.

grounding: Shows a student who sees a cruel post in a huge chat, first assumes someone else will report it, then acts.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Eleven at night in the hostel reading room, Kamal's phone buzzed. The batch group, 312 members. Someone had posted an old photo of Sarita, cropped cruelly, with her room number and a joke about "the ghost of B-block". Laughing reactions piled up: 14, 22, 30.
Kamal glanced across the table. Aditya and Neha were reading it too. Nobody said anything. With three hundred people in there, someone will report it, Kamal thought, and scrolled on.
At midnight the post was still up. Forty-one reactions. Not one message saying take it down.
Kamal's chest felt tight. Her room number was on it. That part wasn't a joke. Kamal reported the post to the group admins, then went down to the warden's office, where the light was still on. "Sir, there's a post with a student's room number on it." The warden read it, phoned the admins and said he would check on Sarita's floor that night.

qa.q: How many members are in the batch group?
qa.a: 312 members.

qa.q: Why did Kamal scroll on at first?
qa.a: With over three hundred people in the group, Kamal felt little personal duty and assumed someone else would report it, until a tight, uneasy feeling set in.

qa.q: What made the room number the point where Kamal had to act?
qa.a: A room number turns mockery into a safety risk, so it needed reporting to the admins and an adult straight away, not a wait.

qa.q: What might it be like for Sarita to see forty-one reactions and no one objecting?
qa.a: Sarita would likely feel humiliated and unsafe, reading the silence of 312 people as proof that nobody was on her side.

grounding: Shows a student who sees a cruel, risky post in a huge group chat and at first assumes someone else will report it.
